Text:
Under the central dogma of molecular biology, genetic information usually flows two ways:

{{c1::DNA → DNA::direction of flow}} — during its transmission from generation to generation

{{c1::DNA → protein::direction of flow}} — during its phenotypic expression in an organism
Back Extra:
Why: DNA → DNA is replication, carried out by a DNA-dependent DNA polymerase; DNA → protein is gene expression, run as transcription and then translation.

Pitfall: usually is doing real work — RNA viruses add two more flows, RNA → RNA and RNA → DNA.

Roster: DNA → DNA (replication) · DNA → protein (transcription, then translation) · RNA → RNA (replication of RNA viruses) · RNA → DNA (RNA tumor virus genome → DNA proviral form)
verified_against: p275: 'According to the central dogma of molecular biology, genetic information usually flows (1) from DNA to DNA during its transmission from generation to generation and (2) from DNA to protein during its phenotypic expression in an organism' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275 (FIGURE 11.1 labels): '1. Perpetuation of genetic information from generation to generation … Replication … DNA-dependent DNA polymerase … 2. Control of the phenotype: Gene expression … Transcription … Translation' | p275: 'During the replication of RNA viruses, information is also transmitted from RNA to RNA.' | p275: 'In addition, genetic information flows from RNA to DNA during the conversion of the genomes of RNA tumor viruses to their DNA proviral forms.'

must_test: usual flow 1: DNA → DNA, during transmission from generation to generation
usual flow 2: DNA → protein, during phenotypic expression in an organism
supporting: the qualifier 'usually' — the RNA-virus flows are the exceptions (sibling card U1_rna_virus_flows)
replication / gene expression as the names of the two flows (FIGURE 11.1 labels, unmarked → Back Extra only)

Text: Genetic information moves from DNA to protein in two steps: (1) {{c1::transcription::process}}, the transfer of information from {{c2::DNA to RNA::direction of flow}}, and (2) {{c1::translation::process}}, the transfer of information from {{c2::RNA to protein::direction of flow}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: in transcription, one strand of the gene's DNA is the template for a complementary RNA transcript (DNA AAA → RNA UUU); in translation, the transcript's nucleotide sequence is converted into the polypeptide's amino-acid sequence by the genetic code (UUU → phenylalanine).

Cue: transcription keeps the language (nucleotides → nucleotides); translation changes it (nucleotides → amino acids).
verified_against: p275: 'The transfer of genetic information from DNA to protein involves two steps: (1) transcription, the transfer of the genetic information from DNA to RNA, and (2) translation, the transfer of information from RNA to protein.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'During transcription, one strand of DNA in a gene is used as a template to synthesize a complementary strand of RNA, called the gene transcript.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'the DNA strand containing the nucleotide sequence AAA is used as a template to produce the complementary sequence UUU in the RNA transcript' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'During translation, the sequence of nucleotides in the RNA transcript is converted into the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide gene product. This conversion is governed by the genetic code, the specification of amino acids by nucleotide triplets called codons in the gene transcript.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'the UUU triplet in the RNA transcript shown in Figure 11.1 specifies the amino acid phenylalanine (Phe) in the polypeptide gene product.'

must_test: transcription = transfer of genetic information from DNA to RNA (two-way: name ↔ direction)
translation = transfer of information from RNA to protein (two-way: name ↔ direction)
the two steps together carry information from DNA to protein (visible frame)
supporting: template strand → complementary transcript; codons → amino acids (unmarked TRANSCRIPTION AND TRANSLATION paragraph → Back Extra only)
AAA → UUU → Phe worked example (unmarked → Back Extra; numeric flag set because the Back Extra states nucleotide sequences, verified against p275)

Text:
Beyond its two usual flows, genetic information also moves two more ways in RNA viruses:

{{c1::RNA → RNA::direction of flow}} — during the replication of RNA viruses

{{c1::RNA → DNA::direction of flow}} — when the genome of an {{c2::RNA tumor virus::virus type}} is converted to its proviral form
Back Extra:
Why: the DNA → RNA step is therefore sometimes reversible, whereas RNA → protein is always irreversible.

Meaning: the proviral form is the RNA tumor virus genome as DNA; the RNA → DNA copying is reverse transcription, done by an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase).

Roster: DNA → DNA (replication) · DNA → protein (transcription, then translation) · RNA → RNA (replication of RNA viruses) · RNA → DNA (RNA tumor virus genome → DNA proviral form)
verified_against: p275: 'During the replication of RNA viruses, information is also transmitted from RNA to RNA.' | p275: 'In addition, genetic information flows from RNA to DNA during the conversion of the genomes of RNA tumor viruses to their DNA proviral forms.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'Thus, the transfer of genetic information from DNA to RNA is sometimes reversible, whereas the transfer of information from RNA to protein is always irreversible.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275 (FIGURE 11.1 labels and caption): 'Reverse transcription … RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase)' and 'reverse transcription occurs in cells infected with certain RNA viruses. The transfer of information from RNA to RNA during the replication of RNA viruses is not shown.'

must_test: RNA → RNA occurs during the replication of RNA viruses
RNA → DNA occurs when RNA tumor virus genomes are converted to their DNA proviral forms
which virus type carries the RNA → DNA flow: RNA tumor viruses (c2)
supporting: 'proviral form' kept visible as scaffolding (the page never defines it beyond 'DNA proviral forms'); the adjective DNA was moved off the front because it names the c1 answer, and the Meaning line restores it after the answer
DNA → RNA sometimes reversible / RNA → protein always irreversible (unmarked follow-on → Back Extra only, as licensed)
skip: virus type of row 1 left visible, not clozed — 'RNA viruses' is derivable from 'RNA → RNA replication' and would be a self-answering row (rule 20)

Text: {{c1::Messenger RNAs (mRNAs)::RNA class}} are the RNA molecules that are {{c2::translated on ribosomes::their fate}}.
Back Extra:
Why: in a eukaryote most genes sit in the nucleus while proteins are made in the cytoplasm, so a messenger is needed to carry the genetic information from the nucleus out to the sites of protein synthesis.

Distinguish: mRNA is the only one of the five RNA classes that is translated — tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA are final products in their own right.
verified_against: p275: 'The RNA molecules that are translated on ribosomes are called messenger RNAs (mRNAs).' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p277: 'If most of the genes of a eukaryote are located in the nucleus, and if proteins are synthesized in the cytoplasm, how do these genes control the amino acid sequences of their protein products? … Messengers are needed to transfer genetic information from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.' | p277: 'Transfer RNA, ribosomal RNA, snRNA, and miRNA molecules are not translated.'

must_test: mRNA = the RNA molecules that are translated on ribosomes (two-way)
supporting: why a messenger is needed: nucleus vs cytoplasm (unmarked p277 → Back Extra only)
mRNA is the only translated class (marks 12–13; the exception itself is carded in U3)
skip: 'codons' (mark 4) and 'primary transcript' (mark 6) — purple lexicon marks, orchestrator's lane

Text: In {{c1::eukaryotes::prokaryotes or eukaryotes}}, the primary transcript usually is a {{c2::precursor to the mRNA}} and so is called a {{c2::pre-mRNA::name}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the primary transcript is the direct product of transcription, before any processing.

Distinguish: in prokaryotes the primary transcript usually is the mRNA — no processing step in between.

Why: eukaryotic primary transcripts often must be processed before they can be translated — specific sequences (the introns) are excised and both ends are modified (a 5′ cap and a 3′ poly(A) tail).
verified_against: p275: 'Thus, in eukaryotes, primary transcripts usually are precursors to mRNAs and, as such, are called pre-mRNAs.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'In prokaryotes, the product of transcription, the primary transcript, usually is equivalent to the mRNA molecule' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'In eukaryotes, primary transcripts often must be processed by the excision of specific sequences and the modification of both termini before they can be translated' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p276 (FIGURE 11.2 caption): 'In eukaryotes, the primary transcripts or pre-mRNAs often must be processed by the excision of introns and the addition of 5′ 7-methyl guanosine caps (Cap) and 3′ poly(A) tails [(A)n].'

must_test: in EUKARYOTES (not prokaryotes) the primary transcript is usually only a precursor to the mRNA (c1, forced choice)
that precursor is called a pre-mRNA (c2 — term and meaning hidden together because each spells the other; the visible anchors 'eukaryotes' + 'primary transcript' still force the answer)
supporting: prokaryote: primary transcript ≈ mRNA (unmarked → Back Extra only)
what processing means: excision of sequences + modification of both termini / cap + poly(A) (unmarked p275–p276 → Back Extra only)
one-clause 'primary transcript' meaning for prerequisite closure (rule 11); the purple lexicon card for mark 6 is the orchestrator's
skip: introns/exons/spliceosome sentence (unmarked here; snRNA card carries it as teaching)

Text:
Five classes of RNA molecule play essential roles in gene expression:

{{c1::mRNA}}, {{c1::tRNA}}, {{c1::rRNA}} — translational roles

{{c1::snRNA}} — splicing

{{c1::miRNA}} — regulation of gene expression
Back Extra:
Why: all five are produced the same way, by transcription — what differs is what happens to the transcript afterwards.

Pitfall: only mRNA is translated; the other four are working RNAs and the final products of their own genes.
verified_against: p276: 'Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are small RNA molecules that function as adaptors between amino acids and the codons in mRNA during translation.' | p276: 'Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are structural and' | p277: 'Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are structural components of spliceosomes, the nuclear organelles that excise introns from gene transcripts.' | p277: 'Micro RNAs (miRNAs) are short 20- to 22-nucleotide single-stranded RNAs' | p277: 'final products of tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and miRNA genes are RNA molecules.' | p277: 'Transfer RNA, ribosomal RNA, snRNA, and miRNA molecules are not translated.' | Stem cue (unmarked, scaffolding only) p276: 'Five different classes of RNA molecules play essential roles in gene expression.' | Stem cue (unmarked, scaffolding only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 caption): 'the splicing function of snRNA, the regulation of gene expression by miRNA, and the translational roles of tRNA, rRNA, mRNA, and ribosomes' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p277: 'All five types of RNA—mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and miRNA—are produced by transcription.'

must_test: membership: the five RNA classes are mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA (rule 30 — can he PRODUCE the five?)
supporting: the source's own grouping (FIGURE 11.3 caption: translational roles / splicing / regulation of gene expression) used as visible row cues so the 5-item group is passable — rule 23 handle = the count 'five' + the caption's three role groups + the shared -RNA suffix; grouping is not clozed (rule 23.1)
all five produced by transcription (unmarked → Back Extra only)
skip: each class's function is its own two-way card in this unit (the row cues here are coarser than those cards' definitions, so this is not the same recall)

Text: {{c1::Transfer RNAs (tRNAs)::RNA class}} are small RNA molecules that function as {{c2::adaptors between amino acids and mRNA codons}} during translation.
Back Extra:
Meaning: a codon is a nucleotide triplet in the gene transcript that specifies one amino acid — the genetic code.

Distinguish: tRNA is the adaptor that pairs an amino acid with its codon; rRNA is the structural and catalytic material of the ribosome that does the translating.
verified_against: p276: 'Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are small RNA molecules that function as adaptors between amino acids and the codons in mRNA during translation.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'the genetic code, the specification of amino acids by nucleotide triplets called codons in the gene transcript' | p276: 'Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are structural and' | p277: 'catalytic components of the ribosomes, the intricate machines that translate nucleotide sequences of mRNAs into amino acid sequences of polypeptides.'

must_test: tRNA = adaptor between amino acids and the codons in mRNA, during translation (two-way)
supporting: 'small' (visible qualifier)
codon meaning for prerequisite closure (unmarked p275 → Back Extra; the purple lexicon card for 'codons' is the orchestrator's)
skip: tRNA structure detail (deferred by the book to Chapter 12, not on these pages)

Text: {{c1::Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs)::RNA class}} are {{c2::structural and catalytic::two roles}} components of the {{c1::ribosomes}}, the intricate machines that translate nucleotide sequences of mRNAs into amino acid sequences of polypeptides.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: snRNAs are also structural components — of the spliceosome, not the ribosome; catalytic is said of rRNA alone.

Cue: keep the word catalytic — rRNA is not mere scaffolding; it takes part in the chemistry the ribosome performs.
verified_against: p276: 'Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are structural and' | p277: 'catalytic components of the ribosomes, the intricate machines that translate nucleotide sequences of mRNAs into amino acid sequences of polypeptides.' | p277: 'Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are structural components of spliceosomes'

must_test: rRNAs are STRUCTURAL and CATALYTIC components of ribosomes ('catalytic' is the recall — c2)

the ribosome is the machine that translates mRNA nucleotide sequences into polypeptide amino-acid sequences; c1 chains machine → its RNA (ribosomes → rRNA) so the name direction is a real recall rather than a 'ribosomal ← ribosome' giveaway
supporting: MARGIN COMMENT on mark 9 ('Add the rest of the sent. Plzzzz') honoured: the whole sentence is carded across the p276/p277 page break and both pages are quoted
the translation definition itself is tested on the U1 two-step card, so the ribosome's job stays visible scaffolding here rather than a duplicate cloze (rule 12)
skip: ribosome composition counts (3–5 RNAs, 50–90 proteins) — unmarked p275 and numeric; left off

Text: {{c1::Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs)::RNA class}} are structural components of {{c2::spliceosomes::organelle}}, the nuclear organelles that {{c3::excise introns}} from gene transcripts.
Back Extra:
Why: introns are noncoding sequences that separate a gene's exons; the whole gene is transcribed into the pre-mRNA, so the introns must be spliced out before it can be translated.

Ex: the spliceosome's snRNAs are named U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6.

Distinguish: rRNA = structural and catalytic, in the ribosome; snRNA = structural, in the spliceosome.
verified_against: p277: 'Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are structural components of spliceosomes, the nuclear organelles that excise introns from gene transcripts.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p275: 'Most of the nuclear genes in higher eukaryotes and some in lower eukaryotes contain noncoding sequences called introns that separate the expressed sequences or exons of these genes. The entire sequences of these split genes are transcribed into pre-mRNAs, and the noncoding intron sequences are subsequently removed by splicing reactions carried out on macromolecular structures called spliceosomes.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 labels, text layer): 'U1 Spliceosome … U4 … U2 U6 … U5' | p276: 'Ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) are structural and' | p277: 'catalytic components of the ribosomes'

must_test: snRNA = structural component of spliceosomes (two-way, c1/c2)
spliceosomes = the nuclear organelles that excise introns from gene transcripts (c3)
supporting: intron/exon meaning for prerequisite closure (unmarked p275 → Back Extra only)
U1/U2/U4/U5/U6 names read off the plate's text layer (names, not values — numeric left false)
skip: 'nuclear' as a cloze — it is inside the class name and would leak from 'nuclear organelles'

Text: Among the RNA classes of gene expression, {{c1::micro RNAs (miRNAs)::RNA class}} are the short RNAs that block the expression of {{c2::complementary or partially complementary::sequence relationship}} mRNAs, by either {{c3::causing their degradation}} or {{c3::repressing their translation}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: a nuclease called Dicer processes the miRNA precursor into the mature miRNA, which acts through RISC (the RNA-induced silencing complex) — either cleavage of the target mRNA or repression of its translation.

Distinguish: snRNA works in the nucleus on the gene transcript (splicing); miRNA works on mRNAs, silencing them.
verified_against: p277: 'Micro RNAs (miRNAs) are short 20- to 22-nucleotide single-stranded RNAs that block the expression of complementary or partially complementary mRNAs by either causing their degradation or repressing their translation.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 caption): 'Dicer is a nuclease that processes the miRNA precursor into miRNA, and RISC is the RNA-induced silencing complex.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 labels): 'RISC … Cleavage of mRNA … Repression of translation' | p277: 'Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are structural components of spliceosomes, the nuclear organelles that excise introns from gene transcripts.'

must_test: miRNAs block the expression of mRNAs (c1: which class does this)
target = complementary or partially complementary mRNAs (c2)
two mechanisms: causing degradation OR repressing translation (c3, grouped pair)
supporting: Dicer / RISC processing chain (unmarked FIGURE 11.3 caption → Back Extra only)
'short' kept visible; the 20–22 nt value and single-strandedness are on the sibling numeric card so they are not shown here

Text: Micro RNAs (miRNAs) are short, {{c2::single::single or double}}-stranded RNAs {{c1::20 to 22 nucleotides::length}} long.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the mature miRNA is cut from a longer precursor (pre-miRNA) by Dicer, a nuclease.

Cue: micro is the size claim — a miRNA is a regulator, not a message; it is never translated.
verified_against: p277: 'Micro RNAs (miRNAs) are short 20- to 22-nucleotide single-stranded RNAs' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 caption): 'Dicer is a nuclease that processes the miRNA precursor into miRNA' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p278 (FIGURE 11.3 label): 'Pre-miRNA' | p277: 'Transfer RNA, ribosomal RNA, snRNA, and miRNA molecules are not translated.'

must_test: miRNA length = 20 to 22 nucleotides (numeric; digits verified against p277 '20- to 22-nucleotide')
miRNAs are single-stranded (forced-choice blank)
supporting: pre-miRNA → Dicer → miRNA (unmarked plate caption → Back Extra only)

Text: Of the five RNA classes, only {{c1::mRNA::RNA class}} is translated into a polypeptide; the final products of the tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA genes are {{c2::RNA molecules::molecule type}}.
Back Extra:
Why: all five classes are produced by transcription — for four of them the transcript itself is the gene's working product, so they are never translated.

Pitfall: not translated does not mean not expressed — tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA are expressed as RNAs that do their own jobs (adaptor, ribosome, spliceosome, silencing).

Cue: 'codes for a protein' and 'is translated' both single out mRNA.
verified_against: p277: 'final products of tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and miRNA genes are RNA molecules.' | p277: 'Transfer RNA, ribosomal RNA, snRNA, and miRNA molecules are not translated.' | p275: 'The RNA molecules that are translated on ribosomes are called messenger RNAs (mRNAs).' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p277: 'Unlike mRNAs, which specify polypeptides, the final products of tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and miRNA genes are RNA molecules.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p277: 'All five types of RNA—mRNA, tRNA, rRNA, snRNA, and miRNA—are produced by transcription.'

must_test: the carve-out: mRNA is the ONLY one of the five that is translated (negator kept loud, exception clozed — recipes §10)
the final products of tRNA, rRNA, snRNA and miRNA genes are RNA molecules (c2)
supporting: marks 12 and 13 are one proposition stated twice ('final product is RNA' ⟺ 'not translated'); Rule 0 + rule 12 → ONE note covering both

c2 is answerable by a reasoning step from the visible carve-out (not translated → the transcript is the product); a non-knower's default answer is 'proteins', which is exactly the misconception the blank catches, so the row is kept
all five produced by transcription (unmarked → Back Extra only)
skip: 'which RNAs are discussed in which chapter' bookkeeping
